newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso asks Congress to pass pension reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso asks Congress to pass pension reform.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, seeking to regain lost political momentum, urged Congress to approve a revamped pension reform bill that was presented to a Senate committee on Tuesday.

The bill, which has been stuck in the legislature for nearly two years, seeks to stem a growing deficit in Brazil's social security system. It is also considered crucial to the long-term prospects of the government's anti-inflation plan.

"Without reform, we will not be able to cure the social security system," Cardoso said in a radio address. He said the current system, which permits some public-sector workers to claim a pension when they are as young as 35, was unjust.

The reform has run into stiff opposition from lawmakers and a powerful civil servants' lobby, which wants to keep generous benefits enshrined in the constitution. In 1996, Brazil spent $17 billion on 873,000 federal pensions while 16.6 million private-sector pensioners shared $40 billion.

Cardoso said the reform would give normal pensioners an extra $3 billion that has been paid every year to "privileged" groups, "the ones who can afford...to run television commercials to pressure lawmakers and prevent them from helping the government."

Last year, the Chamber of Deputies stripped the reform bill of several important points, requiring the government to rewrite it in the Senate. If passed by the senators the bill will return to the deputies for approval of the changes.

Political analysts have doubted whether pension reform and another flagship bill to streamline the civil service are passable as Congress becomes increasingly distracted by the 1998 presidential and congressional elections.

The civil service reform bill, which has also been bogged down by opposition in Congress, faced a decisive week in the lower house where amendments seeking to remove its main points were due to be voted on after two months of delay.

The government's renewed reform push comes after a several dismal months marked by infighting among its allies, corruption scandals and a high-profile demonstration in Brasilia by the radical Landless Movement in April.

Although last week's final approval by Congress of a bill allowing Cardoso to run for re-election next year was seen strengthening the government's hand, there was more bad news on Tuesday when a poll showed that support for its anti-inflation Real Plan had fallen in May.
Of 2,000 people interviewed by private pollsters Ibope, 36 percent described the plan as positive, down from 46 percent in March.
